feedback: If a learner says the dead material 'disappears' or 'rots to nothing', point out that decomposition rearranges matter rather than destroying it — the material moves into the soil, the air, and the decomposers' own bodies, and is all still there.

If a learner describes decomposers only as things that 'eat dead stuff', agree that they do feed on dead matter (so in that sense they are consumers too), then add what sets them apart: as they feed, decomposers break dead remains and wastes down into simple substances released into the soil (and air) that plants can take up again — that release is what closes the loop.

If a learner says plants eat soil or make matter from nothing, explain that roots take in water and mineral nutrients, while the carbon used to make sugars and much of the plant’s dry biomass comes from carbon dioxide in the air through photosynthesis. Matter is taken in and rearranged, not created from nothing.
If a learner thinks energy also cycles back, revisit the energy stream: it enters from the sun and leaks away as heat and never returns, unlike the matter loop.
activities.intendedInsight: A cycle is a literal closed loop: the same matter returns to the beginning and is used again. Decomposers are the load-bearing step that closes the loop; without them nutrients lock up in dead matter. Matter is recycled endlessly, whereas energy flows one way and is transferred out of the ecosystem as dispersed heat, not destroyed.
learnerActions: Follow a single labelled 'parcel' of nutrients as it moves out of the soil, into a growing plant's roots, into an animal that eats the plant, into the animal's dead remains, then into the decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) that break it down and hand the nutrients back to the soil — where the same parcel is taken up by the next plant.
At each step, state what matter is moving and which process moves it.

Turn the decomposers OFF and describe what happens: dead leaves and bodies pile up, nutrients stay locked in dead matter, the soil's available nutrients deplete, and new growth stalls because the loop no longer closes.
Explain in your own words why decomposers are the step that CLOSES the loop and why matter is recycled rather than consumed.
Watch a parallel one-way energy stream — sunlight entering and heat leaking away, never returning — and state the contrast: matter cycles, energy flows.
activities.title: Drive a nutrient parcel around the matter cycle

feedback: If the learner draws a linear chain that stops at dead matter or at the decomposer, prompt: where do those returned nutrients go, and what takes them up next?
If the decomposer node is missing, ask what breaks down the dead matter and returns its nutrients — without it the arrow back to soil has no cause.
Check that labels name both the process and the matter moving, not just the organisms.
activities.intendedInsight: A canonical closed-loop diagram is the shared representation for matter cycling; being able to both read and produce one, with decomposers included, shows the loop actually closes.
learnerActions: Study a labelled cycle diagram of soil → plant → animal → dead matter → decomposer → soil, and for each node and arrow state the process happening and what matter is moving.
Pay particular attention to the decomposer node — describe how fungi, bacteria and worms on a rotting log return nutrients to the soil.
Then construct your own cycle diagram from scratch, ensuring the end arrow feeds back into the beginning so the loop is genuinely closed.
Mark where new plant growth draws on the returned nutrients.
activities.title: Read and build a closed-loop cycle diagram

feedback: Full understanding: matter is conserved and cycles — decomposers return nutrients to soil, taken up by plants, passed to animals, back to decomposers — and the learner can reason about a no-decomposer ecosystem.

Partial: knows decomposers break down dead matter and can trace part of the chain, but treats it as disposal rather than recycling, or cannot close the loop back into new plants — revisit the return-to-soil step.
Gap: thinks rotting matter is destroyed or sees decomposers as mere eaters — re-establish conservation of matter and the recycling role before moving on.

The 'is it destroyed?' question separates learners who think rotting matter vanishes from those who conserve it; the decomposer question separates 'just eats rubbish' from 'recycles nutrients back into the soil'.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can trace the full loop including decomposers, conserves matter, and keeps matter cycling distinct from energy flow. These checks verify the model; they do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing the loop or explaining the decomposer role in their own words.
learnerActions: Sequence the stages of the matter loop in order.
Answer targeted questions such as 'What returns nutrients to the soil?' and sort processes by what they do.
Decide which quantity is recycled and which is lost (matter cycles vs energy flows), and justify the choice.

Respond to this prompt: 'A fallen tree rots away on the forest floor until you can barely see it. Where has all its material gone — is it destroyed? Explain what the decomposers did with it, and how that material can end up in a new plant.'
activities.title: Check and discriminate the model

feedback: Keep the focus on the systems loop: after observing, have the learner place what they saw back onto the cycle diagram so the tangible detail reconnects to the recycling logic.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing real decomposition can make the abstract node tangible and links the systems loop to concrete organisms and to later carbon/water cycle study.
learnerActions: Examine decomposers at work — for example fungi, bacteria and worms on a rotting log, or a short look 'under the soil' at a decomposing layer.
Connect what you observe to the cycle: name what the decomposers are breaking down and what they return to the soil.
Relate this general matter loop forward to the carbon and water cycles you will meet later, which are specific versions of the same idea.
activities.title: Decomposition up close (optional tangible extension)
